standard.title: Work, Income and Identity
standard.description: the reasons individuals work, the types of work they are involved in, and how they may derive an income
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have explored consumer choices and personal financial decision-making (AC9HS6K08). They have encountered the idea that people earn income but have not formally examined the full range of work types, income sources, or the social and identity dimensions of work — including unpaid, volunteer and First Nations community contributions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the reasons individuals work, the types of work they are involved in, and how they may derive an income.

nodes.label: Types of work
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and describe different types of work — full-time, part-time, casual, at home, paid, unpaid, volunteer — and explain that not all work is formally recognised or remunerated.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least four types of work with a concrete example of each; distinguish between paid and unpaid work.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and describe the full range of work types — full-time, part-time, casual, at home, paid, unpaid, unrecognised and volunteer; explain that unpaid and volunteer work contributes to community even when not formally recognised; use examples from students' own communities.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians' management of Country/Place constitutes a form of work — including cultural maintenance, land management and knowledge transmission — that may not be captured in formal employment data
Examine how unpaid domestic work is distributed and valued differently across households, and discuss whether it should be counted in national economic measures
Explore how volunteer work sustains community organisations and services — interview a local volunteer or examine a community organisation's reliance on non-paid contributions
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who only recognise formal paid employment as 'work' will be unable to explain the full range of income sources in the next node, and will miss the social and identity contributions of work that are central to the descriptor's scope. The narrow view also prevents engagement with First Nations and community work contexts.

response_modes.reason: Expanding beyond wage work to include unpaid, volunteer and cultural custodianship work requires multiple concrete examples from different community contexts. Each new context adds a genuinely distinct category to students' understanding of what 'work' encompasses.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of work types across cultural, community, and economic contexts is genuinely broad and includes First Nations cultural maintenance, digital and gig economy work, and informal community contribution — all within Year 7 scope and all pedagogically significant for building an inclusive understanding of work.
success_criteria: Names at least four distinct types of work with an example of each
Distinguishes between paid and unpaid work and explains why both contribute to individuals and communities

nodes.label: How individuals derive an income
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the different ways people derive an income, including wages, salaries, business ownership, dividends, rental income, and social security.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least three ways of deriving income with a concrete example for each; explain the difference between a wage and a salary.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the ways people derive income — working for a wage or salary, owning a business, being a shareholder (dividends), providing a rental service, receiving social security; explain how each income source relates to a different economic role.
wider: Investigate how a First Nations community enterprise generates income for its members and community — examining income streams that combine commercial revenue, grant funding and cultural services
Explore how passive income sources (rental, dividends) differ from active income in terms of economic effort and risk
Examine how gig economy work (e.g. delivery platforms, freelancing) creates income that is neither wage nor salary — and what this means for financial security

response_modes.reason: Students benefit from a growing set of concrete income-source examples before integrating them with work types. Build a class matrix pairing work types with income sources — e.g. volunteer work → no income; rental property owner → rental income.

success_criteria: Identifies at least three different income sources with a concrete example for each
Explains the difference between at least two income sources (e.g. wage vs. business profit)

nodes.label: Reasons for working: identity, community and wellbeing
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the multiple reasons individuals work beyond earning income, including identity, self-esteem, community contribution and material and non-material living standards.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain two reasons individuals work other than earning income, using a specific example for each.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse the contribution work makes to individuals' identity and community roles — including earning income, self-esteem, happiness, community support through volunteering, and material and non-material living standards; apply to a range of work contexts including paid, unpaid and culturally significant work.
wider: Examine how continuity of cultural practices and management of Country/Place contributes to and sustains First Nations communities — analysing how this work contributes to identity, wellbeing and economic sustainability through regional tourism ventures, mentoring and entrepreneurship
Investigate a case where a person chose lower-income work for personal or community reasons — exploring the trade-offs between material and non-material living standards
Analyse how the reasons people work have changed across generations, using evidence from older family members, community data or historical examples

response_modes.reason: Students default to income as the only reason people work. Scaffold explicitly: income is one reason; what else does work provide that money alone cannot? Work through identity, purpose, community belonging and cultural connection as distinct contributions.

First Nations community work — cultural maintenance, mentoring, land management — provides a particularly strong context for seeing non-income motivations as genuine and substantial, not supplementary.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The reasons people work vary meaningfully across cultural and community contexts. First Nations cultural custodianship, volunteer community work, and career choices driven by identity rather than income all offer rich width that deepens students' understanding of work as a multi-dimensional human activity.
success_criteria: Explains at least two reasons individuals work beyond earning income
Uses relevant terms (identity, living standards, material, non-material, volunteer) accurately in explanation
